title: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust
body: Research: parse_number() as a SQLite extension: C vs Rust I was out walking the dog when I got curious about how easy/difficult it would be to write a SQLite C extension that adds a parse_number() function for turning strings like -$1,234.56 or '12.5%' into numeric values that could be summed and sorted. I fired up regular Claude chat (Opus 5.5) and prompted : I'm thinking about a SQLite custom function 'parse_number(value)' that strips ',', '$', '£' and '%', handles a leading '-', and returns 'NULL' for anything it can’t parse Explore the difference between building this as a SQLite extension in C v.s. in Rust - I want to compare performance and code complexity and size of the resulting .so (or whatever) file This gave me a solid starting point - the Rust extension was 321 KB (using Rusqlite ) and 298 KB (using sqlite-loadable-rs ), while the C extension was 14 KB. But the Rust extension was faster! Turns out that's because the Rust equivalent of C's strtod is "twice as fast". title: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages
body: datasette #3046: Don't serve link: rel=next HTTP headers to Firefox for HTML pages I was looking at the Firefox network panel today when I noticed that requests to a Datasette table page were triggering an HTTP prefetch to the next page of rows in that table. This was happening because Datasette pages serve an HTTP link header like this: link: <https://latest.datasette.io/fixtures/compound_three_primary_keys?_next=a%2Cd%2Cv>; rel="next" This is bad. A tiny fraction of the visitors to one of those pages will click the "next" link, which means their browser is fetching unnecessary data and the Datasette server is having to render an entire page that then gets thrown away. I dug in and learned that Firefox has an issue that has been open for 24 years about this behavior... And one of the early comments on that issue links to my blog post from 2002 complaining about this feature. I hadn't just forgotten that I had written about it, I had forgotten the feature entirely! README 節錄：# terminal-mac A separate macOS desktop for computer-use agents, viewed and controlled from a terminal. `terminal-mac` is an early release candidate for Apple silicon. Apple Virtualization runs a real macOS guest. A bundled helper **inside that guest** captures its screen and posts input events. A terminal viewer streams that screen using Kitty or iTerm2 graphics. Agent commands use the same helper without moving the physical Mac's pointer or changing its clipboard. The guest is a separate Mac: it has its own apps, files, accounts and permissions. It does not inherit your running host apps or signed-in sessions. The VM still consumes host CPU, memory and storage. ## Requirements - Apple silicon Mac, macOS 14 or later. - No development tools are needed for a prebuilt release. Maintainers need Xcode 16 or later / Swift 6 to build. - Internet on first run to download macOS directly from Apple, or an existing compatible `.ipsw`. - Space for the cached restore image and a growing VM disk (64 GiB logical size by default). - Ghostty, Kitty or iTerm2 for the inline viewer. Other terminals can use the native VM window and agent CLI. tmux passthrough and automatic terminal splits are not implemented. ## Install and run ```sh curl -fsSL https://github.com/govijr/terminal-mac/releases/latest/download/get.sh | bash ``` The installer downloads the latest release and verifies its SHA-256 before installing. README 節錄：# Ram-Altman **A bash script that writes to Sam Altman once a day to report the RAM he missed.** Read the sample emails at **ram-altman.lol**, no install needed. There is RAM in your computer. Right now. Just sitting there, in a *personal* computer, being personal. You may have thought of this as "a computer working normally". On a recent episode of Cheeky Pint, the CEO of OpenAI offered another view: > "From a global allocation perspective, actually, it's quite terrible to have everybody have a bunch of the world's limited supply of DRAM sitting in their own computer" > > — Sam Altman That RAM, he added, is "being used maybe 5% of the time". Which raised an obvious question for a certain kind of person: *surely someone should be monitoring this?* So we wrote a script. If your machine has more than 10% of its RAM available, it sends one email a day to let Sam know. It seemed only fair. He can't fix the problem if nobody tells him where the RAM is. ## Features - Tracks total, used and available RAM, plus your standing with the global allocation authorities - Handles page cache correctly, which already puts it ahead of most arguments about RAM - Sends at most one email per day, because we're hoarders, not animals - Rotates 8 subject lines, 10 messages and 6 sign-offs, so the joke gets old at a carefully managed pace - Logs every sample to CSV for when the auditors arrive
